segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There are also some variations that you might come across in dialect. For example,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: in most of Spain, they use le and les whenever they're referring to him, or her, or you formal, or you guys, or them.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So instead of lo, and la, and los, and las, they're using le and les.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Not just to make to him, to her, they will use it always when they're referring to people and not things. So in most of Spain,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: le veo means I see him, her, or you formal, and lo veo means I see it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But in the great majority of the Spanish-speaking world, this isn't the case.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In most of Spain, you have vosotros, which is the you plural informal, which is only used in Spain or most of Spain,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: but again nowhere in Latin America. So that might be something you want to listen out for if you will practice this dialect of Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Many accents have an aspirated S in Spanish, so you might hear

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ehta instead of está, ¿cómo ehta? instead of ¿cómo está?, ehpero instead of espero.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Around the Río de la Plata, for example, around Montevideo and Buenos Aires,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and in 30% of the Spanish-speaking world used exclusively or mixed with tú, you also have vos. Vos, another word for tú,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and the verb conjugations might change slightly.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, instead of puedes, you might hear podés.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And because the accent's coming on the end, that O isn't splitting: podés.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Instead of quieres, querés.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, you might come across small differences in different dialects of Spanish, but they are minor. And you now have all of the know-how and experience to identify and understand them. And if you want, adopt them. You can adopt these differences. It's advisable to speak like the people you are practicing with, because the more you speak like the Spanish that you are hearing, the more you understand. Now, if you're talking with people from different Spanish-speaking countries, people with different dialects or accents in Spanish, then you might get something like a pan-Hispanic accent, let's say, like many native Spanish speakers who move around the Spanish-speaking world or spend time with Spanish speakers from different countries also have. You might even find yourself switching between different accents when you're talking with people from different places. Again, a phenomenon that we also find occurring amongst native speakers.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ahora hablamos español. Ahora somos hispanohablantes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now we speak Spanish. Now we are Spanish speakers. Somos hispanohablantes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Y solo tenemos que practicar, hablar, y analizar para perfeccionar nuestro español.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: My advice now for the end of the course is to spend some time practicing, to get out and practice and expose yourself to Spanish as much as possible.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And then maybe after a short while of practicing, you might want to repeat the course to refresh and touch up on anything that you might be unsure of.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Especially having practiced and being solid on so many things, it will really free up a lot of mental space to hone in on the things that you are more uncertain with.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And in this way, repeating the course might be a little bit like when you watch a good movie twice, and on the second time round, you have a different experience.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The most important thing in this journey of exploring and improving your Spanish is to not to forget to enjoy it,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: to not obsess with the destination, but to enjoy the journey. You are already a Spanish speaker, you should enjoy it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There is a huge variety of literature, music, and cinema coming from Spanish-speaking countries, so you can enjoy this and at the same time effectively be studying, but it won't feel like that.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And we must bear in mind also that listening is a separate skill. You will hear many things that you could think your way through and say, and maybe not understand them.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So when you first begin listening, don't be overwhelmed by the fact that you don't understand at the beginning as much as you can speak.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: All you have to do is insist on analyzing the language that you're exposed to, breaking it up and seeing what you can learn from that.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And although at the beginning it will seem very fast, once you get in the habit of this analysis and this breaking up of the language in the same way that we were doing when we were building up to create our sentences,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: in reverse, deconstructing what you hear, the more you do this, the more Spanish will slow down. It will slow right down, and you will hear a lot more.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, like I said, don't be overwhelmed by not understanding a lot at the beginning. Insist,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: enjoy music, watch movies with subtitles, try to match between the subtitles in English and what you are hearing in Spanish, and just try to match bits and pieces.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you insist with this, very quickly you will notice that you are understanding a lot more, and that the language appears to slow right down.
